title: Why a poem
hook: teaching through beauty: he wrote so people would stay for the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashvaghosha himself, and your line: a poet monk. Did your discipline and your delight work together anywhere? Today the poet tells us, in his own words, why he wrote. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

A spoonful of honey, and under it, something bitter. It's an old trick with children: the medicine goes down because something sweet goes with it. It turns out a monk used the same picture to explain why he wrote. At the very end of the poem of Nanda, after all the longing and the journey and the letting go, Ashvaghosha steps out from behind the story and talks to the reader directly. He explains why a monk would write poetry at all.
screen: `HONEY OVER SOMETHING BITTER.` → `THE POET STEPS OUT.` → `WHY WRITE POETRY AT ALL?`

segments.voice: First, the purpose. He says the poem is about liberation, and that he wrote it not to give pleasure but to bring calm. The beauty was never the point. Second, the audience. He says he wrote in this ornate style to catch listeners whose minds are on other things. People who would never sit through a plain teaching might sit through a story with a love affair, a king, a heavenly journey, and stay long enough to hear what it was really about. Third, the honey. And then the picture: just as bitter medicine is mixed with honey so that it can be swallowed, he has mixed the teaching with poetry. Whatever in the poem is about liberation, that's the medicine. The rest, the descriptions, the music of the verse, is there to help it go down. Fourth, the gold. He asks his readers to take what leads to peace and leave the rest, the way someone panning for gold keeps the gold and lets the dust wash away. So the honey is honest about being honey. He isn't hiding the teaching. He's telling you exactly where it is. He said this about the poem of Nanda, but look back at the life we've heard these weeks with the same idea in mind. The empty saddle, the birds in one tree for a night, the dog with a dry bone, the torch of straw. Each one is honey around something hard: parting, grief, craving, and the way out. The poet hoped his listeners would stay for the beauty, and then keep the gold.
screen: `NOT FOR PLEASURE, FOR CALM.` · `FOR MINDS SET ON OTHER THINGS.` · `MEDICINE MIXED WITH HONEY.` · `KEEP THE GOLD, LET THE DUST GO.` · then, large: `BEAUTY CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy one beautiful thing mindfully. Find something beautiful within reach: light on a wall, the sound outside, the color of a cup, a plant, a face in a photo. Look at it, or listen, fully, for a few breaths. Enjoy it. Then, gently, ask what it's carrying. Maybe it says this moment won't last. Maybe it says you're here. Don't force an answer. Let the beauty be the door, and rest in whatever comes through. The bell holds the time.
Why a poem. In his own words, Ashvaghosha wrote for calm, not pleasure, mixing the teaching with verse like medicine with honey. Today's word.
Your line: beauty carries it. Today, when something beautiful stops you, stay one breath longer and ask what it's carrying. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities also teach through story, verse and art: temple murals of the Buddha's life, chanted verses, and retellings of the birth stories, often alongside plain instruction in the teaching.

fork.setup: you have a teaching that can free people, but most of your listeners would rather hear a love story. what do you do?
options: teach it plainly; whoever leaves, leaves.
wrap the teaching inside a beautiful story, and say so.
fork.reveal: Ashvaghosha mixes the teaching with poetry like medicine with honey, then tells readers to keep the gold and let the dust go.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious poetry is decoration.
what it means: for Ashvaghosha the beauty was a way to keep listeners long enough to hear the teaching.
what a scholar hears: he says it himself in the closing verses of the poem of Nanda, with the image of medicine mixed with honey (Saundarananda 18).

sources.ref: Saundarananda 18 (closing verses: written for calm, not pleasure; medicine mixed with honey; gold and dust)

notes: All material paraphrased; no public-domain English translation of the Saundarananda on the validator list.
